title: Durable Objects, Unbound
subtitle: One promised message, a well that learned to say no, and the road to running it yourself
logline: A chat message gets its tick. The machine that gave the tick goes dark. The tick is still true. In a paper-cut harbour town where every machine is a lamp-lit house, a chat room is a lantern and the storage bucket is the town well, the film follows one promised message through every failure that could break it: two houses claiming the room at once, an owner that sleeps and wakes, a crash mid-upload, a successor that dies mid-recovery, a tail that lives only on the neighbours. From Durable Objects in 2020 to the October 2026 commit that began merging celld into workerd, it shows why a bucket that cannot run a line of code can make a room portable, and why it cannot do it alone.

chapters.title: The Tick
chapters.blurb: Cold open on one promised message. Across a made-up harbour, a chat room glows as a paper lantern in House A's window; a sender's slip, the ferry is late, pauses at the lantern's door and gets its tick. Then House A goes dark. Up the hill House C lights, draws the room up from the town well, and the slip still carries its tick. The machine that made the promise is gone; the promise is still true. Down in the square: a storage bucket, which cannot run a line of code, and a brass plate that names the owner. Two old promises, a newer third, and the question the film follows: how can a bucket make a room portable?

chapters.title: One Room in the Whole World
chapters.blurb: 2020 to 2024 on Cloudflare's network. Kenton Varda introduces Durable Objects: one identifier, one place in the world at a time, and a chat room as the demonstration. In 2021 his output gate holds every reply behind a latch until the write it follows has finished: the tick is a held letter, released. In 2022 the runtime, workerd, becomes open source, but its rooms cannot travel: a single instance. In 2024 SQLite moves into the same thread, local reads become almost instant, and Cloudflare's hosted Storage Relay Service keeps the tick honest with object storage and five followers, three to confirm. Real machinery, and all of it inside Cloudflare.

chapters.title: The Well That Learned to Say No
chapters.blurb: The bucket's education, dated. Before December 2020 an overwrite in S3 could be followed by a read of the old copy; then reads became the latest, always. A race with the condition pulled out shows why fresh reads are not enough: an overwrite can win the well, but it cannot take back what was already served. In August 2024 the well learns to refuse a second creation; in November 2024 to refuse a stale replacement: compare and swap. Then the reversal: who referees the referee? Werner Vogels's witness inside S3, proved before it was trusted. celld's warning that a store can look compatible and silently ignore the condition, and the four test writes every node makes before it serves. And the scope: one key, one plate, no promise that two rooms commit as one.

chapters.title: The Plate and the Candle
chapters.blurb: Inside workerd's cluster, as committed on 28 October 2026. The Plate is the ownership record: which house, an epoch, and the last epoch that actually opened. A claim is a compare and swap; a new room is created already open; a remembered route is a shortcut, not proof. Leases are candles: twenty seconds, renewed every three, each attempt allowed four, a clock allowed two seconds of skew and a painted band of four, so a house may serve only while its clock reads under sixteen thousand milliseconds and may start a renewal only under twelve thousand. A comment in the code keeps a scar from real R2 stalls. Then the pin: a keeper falls asleep, its candle burns into the band, a neighbour takes the room; a timeout proves silence, not death, and only the sleeper stopping itself keeps the town to one room. Clocks are borrowed, so celld checks a record, not a clock. And claimed is not opened: the from tile decides which past the room comes back with.

chapters.title: The Ribbon
chapters.blurb: SQLite's write-ahead log, drawn as a ribbon: a thirty-two-byte leader, frames of a twenty-four-byte tab and a page, and on a transaction's last frame a stamp recording the database's size: the commit mark. workerd's keeper cuts the ribbon only after a stamp, so only whole transactions leave the room; rolled-back frames are written over. The cut ribbon goes down to the Well as scrolls tied with checksummed cords, each epoch's shelf starting with a Book; this is workerd's own format, and celld's LTX is a different one. Then the tick itself: upload, a second look at the Plate, and only then the bell. Pull that pin and an old owner rings a bell its successor may never honour. And one honest limit: a lost reply proves nothing either way.

chapters.title: The Neighbours
chapters.blurb: House C rebuilds the room from the Well: it wipes its own copy, reads the newest Book and every scroll in order, and refuses to go on past a missing one. Every workerd tick pays for a trip to the Well. Then the lamps change to celld's town, where the owner's neighbours press each page onto their own disks and the bell can ring before the Well has the page. The tail now lives outside the Well: epoch shelves fence it but cannot recover it, so a successor reads the old owner's log record first, fences it, seals and collects the neighbours' notebooks, uploads them and only then restores. At least one neighbour must certify a complete tail; without one, the room stays shut.

chapters.title: What Travels
chapters.blurb: Every pin we pulled hangs on one board: the Tooth, the candle's band, the second look, the seal. What travels with a room is not the bucket alone but a contract: one-key refusals and fresh reads, a supervisor, and a runtime that cuts, uploads, looks again, seals and replays. The small print, dated 31 October 2026; the announced direction, in the teams' own terms; what the Well will never do. At dawn the lantern burns in House C, and the tick on the sender's slip turns out to be a proof.

Ink bleed from the town into the two desks of 2026 in one frame (geography lock: Kenton Varda's desk screen-left, lamp warm; Ryan Dahl's desk screen-right; beside Ryan Dahl's a second, out-of-focus chair for Bert Belder). Generic, dignified 2020s silhouettes at laptops, no likeness, no gestures toward the town; their hands stay at their desks. Slow dolly in between the two lamps. On 'plan' the two ropes that braided between the desks in ch04 tighten into one braid running out of frame right toward a small paper model of the harbour terrace on a shelf. On 'merged' a paper ribbon labelled with no words passes from Ryan Dahl's side into the braid. The quote appears in a cartouche at upper middle on 'merged', attributed. On 'Well' the camera drifts to the paper harbour model, where a tiny Well sits in its square: on 'run' a tiny keeper's hand stays at the house, not the Well (the Well runs nothing); on 'rooms' two Plates on two separate wells change at different moments, never together; on 'exactly' a bell rings and a ghost repeat hangs beside it; on 'quiet' the Well's rope goes slack and every house closes its own shutters (writers stop; nothing serves on). Name cards are not repeated. Bottom 12% clear.

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: the payoff. Ink bleed from the desks into the canonical town at DAWN (dawnGold): the moon gone low-left, the sea brightening at L1, the far-shore lamps going out one by one as daylight takes over. House C's window holds the Room Lantern, lit; the wellhead badge reads 'workerd · 28 Oct' (unnamed). Slow push from the sea toward the sender at a harbour-side window (L4 right of the Well), phone in hand. On 'tick' the camera settles on the sender's slip #42, 'the ferry is late', its ink tick crisp in the first light (the ch01 image returned). On 'proof' the tick's two strokes trace, as thin gold lines, back to their two sources in one continuous move: the first runs down to the Well, where the bucket holds A's scroll (on 'bytes'); the second rises to the Plate, where a ghost of that night's tiles reads A · 7 · from 7 with the crown lamp lit, and A's bell swings (on 'bell'); then both lines fade into the slip. On 'made' pull back to the whole town in morning light: the three houses, the Well, the Plate, the pulley lines, the sea. End card fades up in the sky above the ridge on 'real' (two lines, centred in the upper third, well clear of the bottom 12%): the pins, then 'Illustrative harbour; real code.' Hold the end card to the end of the shot as the light keeps rising.
